title: Three scripts
note:
Japanese is written with three scripts at once. Hiragana (あいう) writes grammar and native words. Katakana (アイウ) writes foreign words, names and sound effects. Kanji (日本語) carry the meaning of most words.
A word often mixes them: 食べる is the kanji 食 plus the hiragana べる, which change as the verb changes (食べます, 食べた). Those trailing kana are called okurigana.
The little kana printed above kanji are furigana. Nekko only shows them over kanji you haven't learned yet, so you read the kanji themselves.

title: One kanji, several readings
note:
Most kanji have two kinds of reading. The on'yomi came from Chinese and is used mostly in words of two or more kanji: 日本[にほん], 毎日[まいにち]. The kun'yomi is the native Japanese word and is used when the kanji stands alone or has okurigana: 日[ひ] (day, sun).
You don't learn readings in a vacuum: each word tells you which one it uses. Nekko teaches every kanji with its common readings and the words that use them.

title: Marks that change sounds: が, ぱ
note: Two little marks change a kana's sound. ゛ (dakuten) makes it voiced: か ka → が ga, さ sa → ざ za, た ta → だ da, は ha → ば ba. ゜ (handakuten) only goes on the は row and makes a p: は → ぱ pa.

title: Small ゃ ゅ ょ
note: A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ after an い-sound kana blends the two into one beat: き + ゃ = きゃ kya, し + ょ = しょ sho. Compare the full-size version: きや is two beats, ki-ya.

title: Small っ: a pause
note: A small っ doubles the next consonant: you hold a short silent beat before it. がっこう is ga-k-kou, not ga-tsu-kou. In katakana it's ッ: ベッド (bed).

title: Long vowels
note: A vowel can be held for two beats, and the meaning changes: おばさん (aunt) and おばあさん (grandmother). In hiragana you add a vowel kana. A long o is usually written おう and a long e usually えい: せんせい is said sensee. In katakana a dash ー does the job for every vowel.

title: ん and beats
note: Every kana is one beat of the same length, and ん is a full beat of its own. ほん (book) is two beats, ho-n. しんぶん (newspaper) is four. Counting beats is how you hear the difference between きねん (anniversary, three beats) and きんえん (no smoking, four).

title: Foreign words in katakana
note: English words are bent to fit Japanese sounds: every consonant gets a vowel after it, and long sounds get ー. Coffee becomes コーヒー, party becomes パーティー, McDonald's becomes マクドナルド. Combos like ティ, ファ and ウィ exist only for these words.

title: A は B です: "A is B"
note:
The simplest sentence: topic, は, the thing it is, です. です is the polite "is / am / are" and always comes last. Japanese puts the verb (or です) at the end of the sentence.
You leave out "I" and "you" whenever they're obvious, so がくせいです alone means "I'm a student".
ex: わたしはがくせい{です}。
たなかさんはせんせい{です}。

title: は: the topic
note: は marks what the sentence is about: "as for me…". As a particle it's said wa, even though it's written with は (ha). Type wa or ha.
ex: わたし{は}がくせいです。

title: か: questions
note: Put か at the end and a sentence becomes a question. No change in word order, and in writing there's often no question mark.

title: の: of, 's
note: の joins two nouns, like 's or "of": the first one describes the second. わたしのほん is "my book", にほんのくるま "a Japanese car".

title: も: also
note: も means "also, too". It replaces は, が or を: わたしもがくせいです, "I'm a student too".
ex: わたし{も}がくせいです。

title: を: the object
note: を marks what the action is done to: what you eat, read, buy. It's said o, so type o or wo.

title: が: the subject
note: が marks who or what does something, often something new to the conversation: "there's a cat". は sets the topic ("as for…"); が points at the one doing it. Questions with だれ (who) or なに (what) take が, never は.

title: に: at a time, to a place
note: に points at a time (at 7 o'clock, on Monday) or a destination (to school). It also marks where something is: つくえのうえにあります, "it's on the desk".
ex: There's a cat in the room.

title: で: where, and with what
note: で marks where an action happens (eat at home) and what you do it with (go by bus, write with a pen). に is where something is or goes; で is where something is done.

title: へ: towards
note: へ marks a direction, much like に with a destination. As a particle it's said e, so type e or he.

title: と: and, with
note: と joins nouns into a complete list (bread and milk), and marks who you do something with (with a friend).
ex: パン{と}ミルクをかいます。

title: ね and よ
note: These go at the very end and add a tone. ね asks for agreement, like "isn't it?". よ tells the listener something they don't know, like "you know".
ex: これはおいしいです{よ}。

title: Polite verbs: ます, ました, ません
note: Polite verbs end in ます. The ending carries the tense: ます (do, will do), ました (did), ません (don't), ませんでした (didn't). Japanese has no separate future: たべます is "I eat" and "I'll eat".
ex: きのうパンをたべ{ました}。

title: The three verb groups
note:
Dictionary form is how verbs are listed: たべる, のむ. To make the ます form you change the ending, and there are three ways:
• る verbs (ichidan): drop る. たべる → たべます, みる → みます.
• う verbs (godan): the last kana moves to its い-sound. のむ → のみます, かく → かきます, はなす → はなします.
• Two irregular ones: する → します, くる → きます.
A verb ending in いる or える is usually a る verb; anything else is a う verb.

title: い and な adjectives
note: Japanese has two kinds of adjective. い adjectives end in い and go straight before a noun: たかいやま, a tall mountain. な adjectives need な before a noun: しずかなまち, a quiet town. Before です both are plain: やまはたかいです, まちはしずかです.

title: これ, それ, あれ, どれ
note:
A small table worth learning as one. こ- is near me, そ- is near you, あ- is over there, ど- asks which.
• これ それ あれ どれ: this one, that one, that one over there, which one
• この その あの どの + noun: this book, that book…
• ここ そこ あそこ どこ: here, there, over there, where
ex: This (here, by me) is my book.

title: Question words
note: なに / なん (what), だれ (who), どこ (where), いつ (when), どう (how), なぜ / どうして (why), いくら (how much). They sit where the answer would go, and the sentence ends in か.

title: だ: plain "is"
note: だ is the casual form of です, used with friends and in writing. The polite and casual forms of everything come in pairs; Nekko's examples are mostly polite, which is always safe.

title: 1 to 10
note: いち 1, に 2, さん 3, よん (or し) 4, ご 5, ろく 6, なな (or しち) 7, はち 8, きゅう (or く) 9, じゅう 10. Bigger numbers are built like 3 × 10 + 5: さんじゅうご is 35.

ひゃく 100, せん 1,000, まん 10,000. Japanese counts big numbers in ten-thousands, so 100,000 is じゅうまん (ten ten-thousands). A few combinations change sound: さんびゃく 300, ろっぴゃく 600, はっぴゃく 800, さんぜん 3,000, はっせん 8,000.

title: Counting things: ひとつ, ふたつ
note: Things are counted with counter words, not bare numbers. The general counter for things works up to ten: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, とお.
ex: りんごを{ふたつ}ください。
たまごを{ひとつ}たべました。

title: Counting people: ひとり, ふたり, さんにん
note: People take にん, except the first two: ひとり (1 person), ふたり (2 people), then さんにん, よにん, ごにん…
ex: きょうだいは{さんにん}です。

title: Counters that change sound
note: Many counters change sound after 1, 3, 6, 8 and 10. 本 (ほん, long things like pens and bottles): いっぽん, にほん, さんぼん, よんほん, ろっぽん. 匹 (ひき, small animals): いっぴき, にひき, さんびき. 枚 (まい, flat things like paper and tickets) never changes: いちまい, にまい.
ex: ペンが{いっぽん}あります。
ビールを{さんぼん}ください。
きっぷを{にまい}ください。

title: Telling the time
note: じ is o'clock and ふん / ぷん is minutes. Watch the odd ones: よじ (4:00), しちじ (7:00), くじ (9:00); いっぷん, さんぷん, ろっぷん, じゅっぷん. はん is half past.

title: Dates and months
note: Months are number + がつ: いちがつ (January) … but しがつ (April), しちがつ (July), くがつ (September). Days 1 to 10 have their own words: ついたち, ふつか, みっか, よっか, いつか, むいか, なのか, ようか, ここのか, とおか. After that it's number + にち, with はつか for the 20th.

title: Greetings
note:
Set phrases you'll hear every day. They don't break down word by word, so learn them whole.
• おはようございます: good morning (おはよう to friends)
• こんにちは: hello, good afternoon (は said wa)
• こんばんは: good evening
• おやすみなさい: good night
• さようなら: goodbye (for a while); じゃあね / またね to friends

title: Thanks, sorry, please
note:
• ありがとうございます: thank you
• すみません: excuse me, sorry, and also thanks for the trouble
• いただきます: said before eating
• ごちそうさまでした: said after eating
• よろしくおねがいします: "please treat me well", said when meeting someone or asking a favour
• おねがいします: please (when asking for something)
ex: ありがとう{ございます}。
よろしく{おねがいします}。
Nice to meet you / I'm counting on you.

title: あります and います: there is
note: Both mean "there is / I have". います is for living, moving things (people, animals). あります is for everything else, including events. The place takes に.
ex: つくえの上[うえ]に本[ほん]が{あります}。
There's a book on the desk.
こうえんに犬[いぬ]が{います}。
There's a dog in the park.
あした、テストが{あります}。

title: Position words: 上, 下, 中…
note: Positions are nouns joined with の: つくえの上 (on top of the desk), はこの中 (inside the box). 上[うえ] above, 下[した] below, 中[なか] inside, 前[まえ] in front, うしろ behind, となり next to.
ex: はこの{中[なか]}にねこがいます。
There's a cat in the box.
えきの{前[まえ]}でまちます。
I'll wait in front of the station.
いすの{下[した]}にあります。

title: Adjectives: past and not
note:
い adjectives change their い: たかい → たかくない (not tall), たかかった (was tall), たかくなかった (wasn't). The odd one: いい → よくない, よかった.
な adjectives work like nouns: しずかじゃないです, しずかでした.
ex: きのうはさむ{かった}です。
このカレーはから{くない}です。
えいがはよ{かった}です。

title: Plain past: た
note: The casual past swaps the ます form's ました for た. For る verbs that's easy: たべた, みた. う verbs change sound: のむ → のんだ, かう → かった, かく → かいた, いく → いった. する → した, くる → きた.

title: Plain negative: ない
note: The casual "don't". る verbs: drop る, add ない (たべない). う verbs: move the last kana to its あ-sound, add ない (のむ → のまない, かう → かわない). する → しない, くる → こない, and ある → ない.

title: The て form: and then
note: The て form joins actions in order: "I got up and ate". It's made like the plain past with て instead of た: たべて, のんで, かって, かいて, いって, して, きて.
ex: あさおき{て}、ごはんをたべます。
I get up and eat breakfast.
うちにかえっ{て}、ねました。
シャワーをあび{て}、でかけます。

title: てください: please do
note: て form + ください makes a polite request. With a noun, it's を + ください: みずをください, "water, please".
ex: ちょっとまって{ください}。
ゆっくりはなして{ください}。

title: ている: doing now, or a state
note: て form + いる (います) is an action going on ("I'm eating") or a state that lasts ("I live in Tokyo", "I'm married").
ex: いま、ごはんをたべて{います}。
とうきょうにすんで{います}。

title: たい: want to
note: ます stem + たい: "want to do". たべます → たべたい, いきます → いきたい. It works like an い adjective: いきたくない (don't want to go).
ex: にほんへいき{たい}です。
I want to go to Japan.
きょうはでかけ{たくない}です。
I don't want to go out today.

title: ましょう and ませんか: let's
note: ます stem + ましょう is "let's". ませんか ("won't you?") is a softer invitation.
ex: いっしょにたべ{ましょう}。
えいがをみにいき{ませんか}。
Would you like to go see a film?
ちょっとやすみ{ましょう}。

title: に行く: go to do
note: ます stem + に + a motion verb (いく, くる, かえる) says why you go: パンをかいにいきます, "I'm going to buy bread".
ex: パンをかい{に}いきます。
ともだちにあい{に}いきました。
I went to see a friend.

title: から and まで: from, until
note: から is "from" and まで is "until / as far as", for times and places.
ex: くじ{から}ごじまでです。
とうきょう{から}きました。

title: から: because
note: After a sentence, から means "because": the reason comes first. さむいですから、うちにいます, "It's cold, so I'm staying in".
ex: さむい{から}、うちにいます。
It's cold, so I'm staying home.
じかんがありません{から}、タクシーでいきます。
I have no time, so I'll take a taxi.

title: が: but
note: Between two sentences, が means "but". でも at the start of a sentence means the same.
ex: たかいです{が}、おいしいです。
いきたいです{が}、じかんがありません。
I want to go, but I don't have time.

title: 好き and 上手 take が
note: Likes, dislikes, skills and wants mark the thing with が, not を: ねこがすきです, "I like cats". The same goes for じょうず (good at), へた (bad at), わかる (understand) and ほしい (want).
ex: にほんご{が}わかります。
あたらしいくるま{が}ほしいです。

title: より and いちばん: comparing
note: A は B より + adjective: "A is more … than B". B より A のほうが says the same, putting A last. いちばん is "the most": いちばんすきです, "I like it best".
ex: いぬ{より}ねこがすきです。
I like cats more than dogs.
ふゆが{いちばん}すきです。
バスよりでんしゃの{ほう}がはやいです。
The train is faster than the bus.

title: てもいい and てはいけない: may, must not
note: て form + もいいです is "you may", and with か it asks permission. て form + はいけません is "you must not".
ex: はいって{も}いいですか。
ここでたべて{は}いけません。
しゃしんをとって{も}いいです。

title: ないでください: please don't
note: ない form + でください asks someone not to do something.
ex: ここでたばこをすわ{ないで}ください。
わすれ{ないで}ください。

title: まえに and あとで: before, after
note: Dictionary form + まえに is "before doing". た form + あとで is "after doing". With nouns: しょくじのまえに, しょくじのあとで.
ex: ねる{まえに}、はをみがきます。
I brush my teeth before bed.
しゅくだいをした{あとで}、あそびます。
I'll play after doing my homework.

title: とき: when
note: とき (time) after a noun with の, an adjective, or a verb means "when …": こどものとき, "when I was a child".
ex: こどもの{とき}、よくあそびました。
I played a lot when I was a kid.
ひまな{とき}、ほんをよみます。

title: なる: become
note: なる is "become". い adjectives turn い into く: さむくなります (it's getting cold). Nouns and な adjectives take に: せんせいになりたい, しずかになりました.
ex: せんせいに{なりたい}です。
I want to become a teacher.
へやがきれいに{なりました}。

title: でしょう: probably
note: でしょう at the end means "probably", as in weather forecasts. With a rising tone it asks for agreement: "right?".
ex: あしたはあめ{でしょう}。
たのしかった{でしょう}。

title: や: and so on
note: や lists a few examples out of more: パンやミルク, "bread, milk and so on". と lists everything; や hints there's more. など (etc.) often closes the list.
ex: パン{や}ミルクをかいました。
I bought bread, milk and so on.
きょうとやなら{など}にいきました。
I went to Kyoto, Nara and other places.

title: もう and まだ: already, not yet
note: もう + past is "already". まだ + negative is "not yet": まだです alone answers "not yet".

title: だけ: only
note: だけ goes after what it limits: ひとりだけ, "just one person".

title: ことができる: can do
note: Dictionary form + ことができる is "can do". こと turns the verb into a thing, and できる is "be possible".
ex: にほんごをはなす{こと}ができます。
ここでおよぐことが{できません}。
